report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that food-grade wax coatings on apples cause cancer is **false**. 

### Summary of Evidence
* **Origin of the Claim:** Rumors that apple wax causes cancer stem primarily from viral internet videos and social media posts, rather than scientific studies or evidence-based research [https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/wax-on-apples-causes-cancer/].
* **Safety & Regulatory Approval:** Food-grade waxes applied to apples—commonly including carnauba wax, shellac, or beeswax—are approved by regulatory agencies like the FDA and are considered safe for consumption [https://www.yahoo.com/lifestyle/worried-wax-apples-191508007.html].
* **Function of Wax:** Apples naturally produce a protective waxy layer ("bloom") to retain moisture. Commercial washing removes part of this natural layer, so packers reapply a minute amount of food-grade wax to prevent spoilage and extend shelf life [https://scienceinsights.org/what-is-the-wax-on-apples-and-is-it-safe-to-eat/].
* **Expert Consensus:** Food safety experts and fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked claims linking food-grade apple waxes to cancer or toxicity [https://www.memesita.com/are-waxed-apples-safe-the-truth-about-apple-coatings/]. Consumers who prefer to avoid added coatings can easily wash or peel their apples.
